title: Parsing a whole sentence

objectives.can: Work through a long sentence in order: find the finite verbs, mark the clauses, attach participles and infinitives, and say what each case is doing.

explanation.summary: A long Greek sentence is read in a fixed order of questions: where is the main verb, which words open subordinate clauses, what does each participle and infinitive belong to, and what job does each case do. This lesson sets out the method and works it on three sentences, from Luke, Romans and Hebrews.

sections.heading: A method in seven steps
body: 1. Find the end of the sentence. A full stop (.) or the Greek question mark (;) ends it. A raised point (·) sometimes ends a sentence and sometimes only a clause, and a comma never ends one.
2. Mark every finite verb: a verb with a person and a number. Infinitives and participles are not finite. Each finite verb belongs to its own clause.
3. Decide which finite verb is the main one. It is usually not in a relative clause, a clause with ὅτι or ἵνα, or a time clause. It may come late: the sentence can hold the reader waiting.
4. Mark each word that opens a subordinate clause: a relative pronoun, a conjunction (ἐπειδήπερ, καθώς, ἵνα, ἕως, ὅτι), or a participle phrase.

5. Attach each participle and infinitive. A participle agreeing with the subject of a verb belongs to that verb. A participle with the article belongs to a noun. An infinitive completes a verb or follows a preposition with the article.

6. Say what each case is doing. Nominative: subject or predicate. Accusative: object, or the subject of an infinitive. Genitive: of, or a part of a genitive absolute. Dative: to, for, with, in. A noun in the vocative addresses someone.
7. Read the sentence again in Greek order, one piece at a time, and say what each piece adds. The order of the Greek is the order in which the writer meant it to be heard.

sections.heading: Worked sentence 1: Luke 1:1–4
body: Luke 1:1–4 is one sentence. It has five finite verbs: ἐπεχείρησαν in verse 1, παρέδοσαν in verse 2, ἔδοξε in verse 3, and ἐπιγνῷς and κατηχήθης in verse 4. Which is the main verb? Not ἐπεχείρησαν, which is in the clause that begins Ἐπειδήπερ. Not παρέδοσαν, which is in the clause that begins καθώς. Not ἐπιγνῷς, which is in the clause that begins ἵνα, nor κατηχήθης, which is inside the relative clause within it. The main verb is ἔδοξε, 'it seemed good', and it does not appear until the third verse.

Everything before it is preparation. Ἐπειδήπερ πολλοί ἐπεχείρησαν ἀνατάξασθαι: the subject is πολλοί, and ἀνατάξασθαι is an infinitive completing ἐπεχείρησαν. The clause then goes on with διήγησιν as its object and a genitive plural phrase, τῶν πεπληροφορημένων … πραγμάτων, in which the participle agrees with πραγμάτων. Verse 2 adds a καθώς clause, 'just as those who were eyewitnesses and servants of the word handed them on to us'. After all this, verse 3 gives the main clause: ἔδοξε κἀμοί, 'it seemed good also to me', with the perfect participle παρηκολουθηκότι agreeing with the dative κἀμοί, and the infinitive σοι γράψαι telling what seemed good. Verse 4 is a purpose clause, ἵνα ἐπιγνῷς, which contains the relative clause περὶ ὧν κατηχήθης λόγων.

sections.heading: Worked sentence 2: Romans 1:1–4
body: Romans 1:1–4 is the opening of a longer sentence. It has only one finite verb, προεπηγγείλατο in verse 2, and that verb is inside a relative clause. So the greeting has no main verb of its own. It names the sender, describes him, and describes the gospel and the Son it concerns. The reader must therefore trace what each phrase hangs on.

Παῦλος is the subject. Three more words describe him in the nominative, δοῦλος, κλητὸς ἀπόστολος and the perfect participle ἀφωρισμένος, all agreeing with Παῦλος. The participle introduces εἰς εὐαγγέλιον θεοῦ, 'for the gospel of God'. The relative ὃ, neuter singular, refers back to εὐαγγέλιον and begins a clause with the verb προεπηγγείλατο. Verse 3 continues with περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ, and then τοῦ γενομένου, an articular participle in the genitive agreeing with υἱοῦ. Verse 4 adds another one, τοῦ ὁρισθέντος, and ends with a string of genitives, Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν, which stand in apposition to the Son already named. How best to translate ὁρισθέντος, and how to take ἐν δυνάμει, are matters on which commentators differ; the grammar here fixes only what the participle agrees with.

sections.heading: Worked sentence 3: Hebrews 1:1–2
body: Hebrews 1:1–2 shows a different pattern: the subject comes first and the verb waits. In verse 1, ὁ θεός is followed by the aorist participle λαλήσας, which agrees with it in the nominative, and by a string of adverbs and prepositional phrases. The finite verb is in verse 2, ἐλάλησεν. So the participle is read with the main verb: God, having spoken in the past in many ways, spoke to us in a Son.

Verse 2 then adds two relative clauses on υἱῷ. The first is ὃν ἔθηκεν κληρονόμον πάντων: ὃν is accusative singular masculine, the object of ἔθηκεν, and κληρονόμον is a second accusative saying what he was appointed. The second is δι' οὗ καὶ ἐποίησεν τοὺς αἰῶνας: οὗ is the genitive after διά, and καί means 'also'. Each relative gets its gender and number from υἱῷ and its case from its own clause.

sections.heading: What to expect from a method
body: The seven steps give a first reading. They do not settle every question. Where a participle could belong to either of two verbs, where a genitive could depend on either of two nouns, or where a prepositional phrase could modify either a verb or a noun, readers and commentators differ. In such places say what the choices are, and prefer the one the grammar and the sense support best. A good habit is to write down the structure before you translate.

misunderstandings: Taking the first finite verb as the main verb. A sentence may begin with subordinate clauses, and the main verb may wait, as ἔδοξε does in Luke 1:3.
Reading a participle as a finite verb. A participle never has a person; a participle in the nominative agreeing with the subject still belongs to the verb it modifies.
Stopping at every comma. A comma does not end a Greek sentence, and long ones run through several verses.
Translating before parsing. English word order hides the structure that the Greek order shows.

deeper.heading: Periods in Greek prose
body: Teachers of Greek rhetoric spoke of the 'period', a sentence built of balanced parts that holds the reader's attention until the end. Luke 1:1–4 is often cited as a New Testament example of a period in the literary style. Ephesians 1:3–14, in the editions that read it as one sentence, is a different kind: a chain of clauses joined by relatives and participles, with no balanced construction. The same method works for both.

deeper.heading: Punctuation is editorial
body: The oldest manuscripts have little or no punctuation. The commas, raised points and full stops in any edition are the editor's decisions, and different editions divide some sentences differently. This lesson follows the text of this library, and the method does not depend on its punctuation.

examples.analysis: Ἐπειδήπερ opens a subordinate clause. πολλοί, nominative plural, is its subject, ἐπεχείρησαν is its finite verb, and ἀνατάξασθαι is an infinitive completing it, with διήγησιν as the object. The perfect passive participle πεπληροφορημένων has the article and agrees with the genitive plural πραγμάτων. Nothing here is the main verb: the sentence is still waiting.

The ἵνα clause of verse 4 follows as the purpose.

practice.prompt: Luke 1:1–4 is one sentence. In verse 3, ἔδοξε κἀμοὶ παρηκολουθηκότι … σοι γράψαι. Which word is the main verb of the whole sentence?

options: ἔδοξε, because the other finite verbs are in subordinate clauses opened by Ἐπειδήπερ, καθώς and ἵνα
ἐπεχείρησαν, because it is the first finite verb
παρέδοσαν, because it has the nearest subject
practice.explain: The first finite verb is in an Ἐπειδήπερ clause, the second in a καθώς clause, and the last two in a ἵνα clause and the relative clause inside it. ἔδοξε is the only finite verb that is not inside a subordinate clause.

There is no subject: παρέδοσαν is impersonal
The subject is τοῦ λόγου, and γενόμενοι is its verb
check.explain: παρέδοσαν is third plural, and the nominative plural οἱ … αὐτόπται καὶ ὑπηρέται is its subject. γενόμενοι is a nominative plural participle agreeing with that subject. ἡμῖν is dative: 'to us'.

check.prompt: ἔδοξε κἀμοὶ παρηκολουθηκότι ἄνωθεν πᾶσιν ἀκριβῶς. In what case is παρηκολουθηκότι (word 2), and with what does it agree?

check.explain: The form is a perfect active participle in the dative singular. κἀμοί (καὶ ἐμοί) is dative singular, 'to me also', so the participle describes the person to whom it seemed good. πᾶσιν is dative plural and does not match in number.

check.prompt: ἵνα ἐπιγνῷς περὶ ὧν κατηχήθης λόγων τὴν ἀσφάλειαν. What does the clause that begins ἵνα do in the whole sentence?

options: It is the main clause of the sentence
It is a time clause: 'when you know'
It states the purpose of writing, and it contains a relative clause περὶ ὧν κατηχήθης λόγων
check.explain: ἵνα with the subjunctive ἐπιγνῷς gives the purpose of the infinitive σοι γράψαι in verse 3. Inside it, ὧν is a relative pronoun whose antecedent noun λόγων stands in the clause. The main clause is ἔδοξε.

check.prompt: ἔδοξε κἀμοὶ … σοι γράψαι. What is the job of the infinitive γράψαι (word 8)?

options: It is a noun meaning 'a writer'
It gives the time of ἔδοξε
It says what seemed good: it completes ἔδοξε, and σοι is the person written to
It is the main verb, and ἔδοξε is its subject
check.explain: ἔδοξε is an impersonal verb that needs a second verb to say what seemed good. The infinitive supplies it, and the dative σοι is the indirect object of 'write'. The infinitive is not finite.

check.prompt: Romans 1:1–4 has a long run of nominatives, participles and genitives. How many finite verbs does it contain?

options: None: every verb is a participle
One: προεπηγγείλατο, in a relative clause
check.explain: Verse 1 has the participle ἀφωρισμένος, verse 2 the finite verb προεπηγγείλατο, and verses 3 and 4 the participles γενομένου and ὁρισθέντος. The only finite verb is inside the relative clause ὃ προεπηγγείλατο.

check.prompt: περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ, τοῦ γενομένου ἐκ σπέρματος Δαυὶδ κατὰ σάρκα. With what noun does the articular participle τοῦ γενομένου (words 4–5) agree?

options: υἱοῦ (word 2): both are genitive singular masculine, and the participle describes the Son
check.explain: τοῦ γενομένου is genitive singular masculine, with the article, so it is an adjective-like phrase on a genitive masculine noun. υἱοῦ fits; σπέρματος is neuter, and σάρκα is accusative feminine.

options: As an apposition: they name the Son who is described in verses 3 and 4
As the object of ἐν δυνάμει
check.explain: The genitive phrase repeats the person in another form: it stands in apposition to the Son. The sentence has no genitive absolute, because there is no participle with a subject of its own in the genitive.

check.prompt: ἐν υἱῷ, ὃν ἔθηκεν κληρονόμον πάντων. What are the case and job of ὃν (word 9)?

options: Genitive plural: it depends on πάντων
Nominative singular masculine: the subject of ἔθηκεν
Dative singular: it agrees with υἱῷ in case
Accusative singular masculine: the object of ἔθηκεν, referring to υἱῷ
check.explain: The relative takes its gender and number from υἱῷ (masculine singular) and its case from its own clause, where it is the object of ἔθηκεν. The subject of ἔθηκεν is God, the same subject as ἐλάλησεν. κληρονόμον is a second accusative saying what he was appointed.

options: Translate the first clause and go on to the next
Look up every noun in a lexicon
Find the end of the sentence and mark every finite verb, then decide which is the main one
Stop at the first comma and parse what is before it
check.explain: Finite verbs show how many clauses there are, and the main verb shows which clause is at the top. Without that map, a translation of the first clause can mislead, as it would in Luke 1:1–4, where the main verb comes in verse 3.

reading.why: One long, carefully built sentence in four verses, with a clause opened by Ἐπειδήπερ, a καθώς clause, a main verb that waits until verse 3, an infinitive, a perfect participle, a vocative and a ἵνα clause that holds a relative clause.
